text: Problem §1 Introduction, §2 Background In 2017 sequence transduction, translation above all, was dominated by recurrent encoder-decoders (LSTMs and GRUs), usually with an attention mechanism between encoder and decoder, and by convolutional alternatives such as ByteNet and ConvS2S ( §1 , §2 ).
label: core

text: A recurrent network computes its hidden state h t from h t −1 and the input at position t , so training cannot be parallelised along the sequence: that caps how much of a GPU a batch can use, and memory limits batching across examples as sentences get longer.
label: core
key: training cannot be parallelised along the sequence

text: Convolutional models do compute all positions in parallel, but connecting two distant positions takes a stack of layers, O( n / k ) for contiguous kernels (ConvS2S) or O(log k n ) for dilated ones (ByteNet), so long-range dependency paths stay long ( §4 ).
label: core

text: The question: can attention alone, with no recurrence and no convolution, carry an entire sequence model?
label: core

text: Idea §4 Why Self-Attention, Table 1 Let every position look at every other position directly, in one step.
label: core
key: Let every position look at every other position directly

text: Section 4 compares layer types on three counts: total computation per layer, how much of it can run in parallel (the minimum number of sequential operations), and the longest path a signal has to travel between two positions, since shorter paths make long-range dependencies easier to learn ( §4 , Table 1 ).
label: core
key: the longest path a signal has to travel

text: Layer Computation per layer Sequential operations Longest path Self-attention O( n ²· d ) O(1) O(1) Recurrent O( n · d ²) O( n ) O( n ) Convolutional O( k · n · d ²) O(1) O(log k ( n )) Self-attention, restricted to r neighbours O( r · n · d ) O(1) O( n / r ) n is the sequence length, d the representation size, k the kernel width, r the neighbourhood size ( Table 1 ).
label: core

text: When n < d , as with sentence-level word-piece and byte-pair tokens, self-attention is also cheaper per layer than recurrence: n ² d < nd ² exactly when n < d , so with the base model's d = 512 the crossover is at 512 tokens.
label: core

text: The paper also suggests restricting attention to a neighbourhood of size r for very long sequences, at the price of an O( n / r ) path ( §4 ).
label: core
key: for longer sequences the paper suggests the restricted row

text: Method: scaled dot-product attention §3.2.1, Eq.
label: core

text: 1 The Transformer is an encoder-decoder built only from attention, position-wise feed-forward layers, residual connections and layer normalisation ( §3 ).
label: core
key: built only from attention, position-wise feed-forward layers

text: Attention maps a query and a set of key-value pairs to a weighted sum of the values, the weights coming from how well the query matches each key.
label: core

text: With queries and keys of size d k and values of size d v , packed as matrices: Attention( Q , K , V ) = softmax( QK ⊤ / √ d k ) V Equation 1 ( §3.2.1 ).
label: core

text: Dot-product rather than additive (Bahdanau) attention, because it is a single matrix multiply: similar in theory, much faster and more memory-efficient in practice.
label: core

text: The 1/√ d k is the load-bearing detail.
label: core

text: If the components of q and k are independent with mean 0 and variance 1, then q · k = Σ q i k i has mean 0 and variance d k (the paper's footnote 1).
label: core

text: Unscaled, the logits spread out as d k grows and push the softmax into regions with tiny gradients; the paper notes that additive attention beats unscaled dot-product attention at large d k ( §3.2.1 ). without the 1/√d k , what happens to the largest attention weight over 10 keys as d k grows from 4 to 512?
label: core
key: additive attention beats unscaled dot-product attention

text: It stays about the same It heads towards 1: one key takes all the weight It falls towards 1/10: the weights flatten out Try: these are real random vectors, drawn fresh with each press of Redraw.
label: core

text: Drag d k up and watch the unscaled softmax (left) collapse onto one key while its gradient vanishes; the scaled one (right) keeps the same spread at every size. d k = 64 Redraw vectors Ten keys and one query with components drawn from a standard normal (Box-Muller, seeded).
label: core

text: Variance of q · k is measured over 4,000 fresh pairs. "Largest gradient" is the largest entry of the softmax Jacobian, max p i (1 − p i ) : how much the strongest logit can still move the output.
label: core

text: Illustrative inputs; the formula is the paper's.
label: core
key: Illustrative inputs; the formula is the paper's

text: Method: multi-head attention §3.2.2 Instead of one attention over d model = 512 dimensions, the queries, keys and values are projected h = 8 times with learned matrices W i Q , W i K ( d model × d k ) and W i V ( d model × d v ), with d k = d v = d model / h = 64 .
label: core

text: Each head runs attention in parallel; the h outputs are concatenated and projected back by W O ( hd v × d model ) ( §3.2.2 ).
label: core

text: MultiHead( Q , K , V ) = Concat(head 1 , …, head h ) W O , head i = Attention( QW i Q , KW i K , VW i V ) Because each head is h times narrower, the total cost is about that of one full-width head.
label: core
key: the total cost is about that of one full-width head

text: What it buys: heads can attend to different subspaces and positions at once, where a single head has to average them.
label: core
key: different subspaces and positions at once

text: In the ablation one head costs 0.9 BLEU against the best setting (24.9 against 25.8), and too many heads hurt as well: 32 heads of 16 score 25.4 ( Table 3 rows (A) ).
label: core

text: The Run a Transformer tab shows every head of a trained toy model, and a one-head version of it.
label: core
key: shows every head of a trained toy model

text: Method: the block (post-LN) §3.1, §3.2.3, §3.3, §3.4 The encoder is a stack of N = 6 identical layers with two sub-layers each: multi-head self-attention, then a position-wise feed-forward network.
label: core
key: identical layers with two sub-layers each

text: Every sub-layer is wrapped as LayerNorm( x + Sublayer( x )) , normalisation after the residual sum ("post-LN"), with dropout on the sub-layer output before it is added.
label: core

text: Every sub-layer and the embeddings produce outputs of size d model = 512 so the residuals line up ( §3.1 , §5.4 ).
label: core

text: The decoder is also N = 6 layers, with three sub-layers: masked self-attention , where every illegal connection is set to −∞ before the softmax so position i sees only positions up to i (combined with the outputs being shifted right by one, a prediction depends only on earlier words); cross-attention , whose queries come from the decoder and whose keys and values come from the encoder's output, so every output position can look at every input position; and the same feed-forward network ( §3.1 , §3.2.3 ).
label: core
key: every illegal connection is set to

text: The base model's layout, from Figure 1 : N = 6 of each layer, d model = 512, h = 8, d ff = 2048.
label: core

text: Add & Norm is LayerNorm( x + Dropout(Sublayer( x ))).
label: core

text: FFN( x ) = max(0, xW 1 + b 1 ) W 2 + b 2 Equation 2 ( §3.3 ): the same two linear maps with a ReLU between them at every position (two convolutions of kernel size 1), different from layer to layer; inner size d ff = 2048, a 4× expansion.
label: core

text: One weight matrix is shared by the input embedding, the output embedding and the pre-softmax projection, and in the embedding layers it is multiplied by √ d model ( §3.4 ); with the shared English-German vocabulary of about 37,000 tokens, that one matrix is 18.9 million of the base model's parameters (37,000 × 512, counted in the tables tab ).
label: core
key: 18.9 million of the base model's parameters

text: Method: positional encoding §3.5 With no recurrence and no convolution nothing in the model knows word order, so it has to be injected.
label: core
key: nothing in the model knows word order

text: The paper adds fixed sinusoids to the embeddings at the bottom of both stacks: PE ( pos , 2 i ) = sin( pos / 10000 2 i / d model ), PE ( pos , 2 i +1) = cos( pos / 10000 2 i / d model ) Each dimension is a sinusoid; the wavelengths form a geometric progression from 2π to 10000 · 2π ( §3.5 ).
label: core

text: Why sinusoids: for any fixed offset k , PE pos + k is a linear function of PE pos (each sine and cosine pair is rotated by an angle that depends only on k ), which the authors hoped would make attending by relative position easy to learn.
label: core
key: attending by relative position easy to learn

text: Learned absolute embeddings gave nearly identical results (25.7 BLEU against 25.8, Table 3 row (E) ); the sinusoids were kept because they might extrapolate to sequences longer than any seen in training ( §3.5 ).
label: core

text: Left: the encoding of positions 0 (top) to 63 (bottom) across all 512 dimensions at d model = 512 (blue negative, orange positive): fast sinusoids on the left, wavelengths up to 10000 · 2π on the right.
label: core

text: Right: PE p · PE p + k against the offset k for three starting positions p : the curves coincide, because the dot product depends only on the offset.
label: core
key: the dot product depends only on the offset

text: Optimiser ( §5.3 ): Adam with β 1 = 0.9, β 2 = 0.98, ε = 10 −9 , and a learning rate that rises linearly for 4,000 warmup steps, then falls with the inverse square root of the step (Equation 3, below).
label: core

text: Regularisation ( §5.4 ): residual dropout 0.1 on every sub-layer output and on the sums of embeddings and positional encodings (0.3 for the big English-German model); label smoothing ε ls = 0.1, which "hurts perplexity, as the model learns to be more unsure, but improves accuracy and BLEU".

text: Why it matters beyond the paper: later work, each claim linked This is the architecture paper of the deep learning era.
label: fat
note: wind-up ("the architecture paper of the deep learning era")

text: Removing recurrence made training embarrassingly parallel across sequence length, which let compute be spent on model and data size instead of waiting on wall-clock sequential steps.
label: core

text: Every frontier LLM (GPT, Claude, Llama, Gemini, DeepSeek), BERT-style encoders, ViT, CLIP, Whisper and most of diffusion's backbone work descend from this design.
label: core

text: What modern stacks changed since 2017 is a checklist of the paper's choices that turned out not to be load-bearing; the Then and now tab morphs the 2017 block into a 2026 one step by step, each step with its paper: Pre-LN instead of post-LN (the norm before each sub-layer) for stable training without the warmup sensitivity; LayerNorm itself usually replaced by RMSNorm.
label: core
key: pre-LN and RMSNorm replaced post-LN LayerNorm

text: RoPE instead of sinusoidal absolute encodings (rotary embeddings applied inside attention), plus interpolation and YaRN tricks to extend the context.
label: owned:models_and_training/topic_llm_architecture/positional_encodings

text: SwiGLU or GeGLU instead of ReLU in the FFN, bias terms dropped.
label: core
key: SwiGLU (or GeGLU) replaced the ReLU FFN

text: Decoder-only, not encoder-decoder : GPT-style causal language models won for generation; cross-attention survives mainly in multimodal adapters and encoder-decoder holdouts (T5, Whisper).
label: core

text: Attention efficiency : MQA, GQA and MLA shrink the KV cache; FlashAttention makes exact attention IO-aware; the O( n ²) cost the paper acknowledged is now the central serving bottleneck (PagedAttention, sliding windows, sparse and linear hybrids such as Mamba).
label: owned:models_and_training/topic_llm_architecture/attention_variants

text: Regularisation and optimiser : label smoothing and heavy dropout largely dropped at pretraining scale (PaLM trained without dropout); the warmup then decay schedule survives in cosine form (GPT-3: linear warmup over 375M tokens, cosine decay to 10%), and Adam's β 2 moved from 0.98 to 0.95 ( GPT-3, Appendix B , PaLM §5 ).
label: core

text: What survived untouched: scaled dot-product attention itself, multi-head projections, and the residual-plus-norm wrapping.
label: core

text: Two items the older version of this page listed as untouched have moved: the 4× FFN expansion survives as a parameter budget, not a shape (a SwiGLU FFN has three matrices, so it uses an inner size near 8/3 × d , or 3 to 3.5 × in Qwen3 8B and Llama 3.1 8B), and weight-tied embeddings survive in small models (Llama 3.2 1B, Qwen3 0.6B) while large ones untie them (Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen3 8B, DeepSeek-V3), as their config files show (the Then and now tab links them).
label: depth

text: BERT kept the encoder; GPT-3 and Scaling Laws scaled the decoder; T5 kept the encoder-decoder; ViT fed it image patches; RoFormer replaced its positional encoding; FlashAttention and PagedAttention attack the memory and IO costs it created; Mamba tries to remove its O( n ²) core.
label: core

label: depth

section: run a transformer: a real model, built and trained like the paper's
text: Training : 16,000 steps of 128 sentences generated on the fly; Adam β 1 0.9, β 2 0.98, ε 10 −9 ; Equation 3's schedule with warmup 4,000; residual and embedding dropout 0.1; label smoothing 0.1; seed 7; about 11 minutes per model on a laptop CPU.
label: depth

section: run a transformer: a real model, built and trained like the paper's
text: Shipping : matrices quantised to 6 bits per weight with one scale per row (one base64 character per weight), vectors in float16: 38,858 characters per model, 117 KB for all three, inside this page.
label: depth

label: depth

section: run a transformer: a real model, built and trained like the paper's
text: Check : on 200 held-out sentences the JavaScript forward pass and PyTorch on the same weights give identical translations for all three models, logits within 1.1 × 10 −5 and attention weights within 1.2 × 10 −6 (check_forward.py).
label: depth

text: Differences from the paper : greedy decoding instead of beam 4, no checkpoint averaging, synthetic data, and toy sizes; everything else follows §3 and §5 .
